nameStory: The cannonball jelly gets its name from its remarkably spherical, dome-shaped bell that looks just like an old-fashioned cannonball floating through the water. When you spot one drifting near the surface, the resemblance is so striking that early observers couldn't help but think of naval artillery! It's also sometimes called the cabbagehead jellyfish, though the cannonball comparison seems to have stuck better.
description: The cannonball jelly is a distinctive, dome-shaped jellyfish that looks remarkably like its namesake floating through the water. Its bell can grow up to 10 inches across, making it one of the more substantial jellies you might encounter. Unlike the classic jellyfish with long, trailing tentacles, this species has a cluster of short, thick oral arms underneath its bell that help it swim and catch food. The rim of its dome is often tinged with brown coloring, giving it additional character.

idTips.label: Dome shape
idTips.description: The bell is perfectly round and dome-shaped, just like a cannonball - smooth and firm-looking rather than flat or saucer-like

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Can reach up to 10 inches in diameter, making it quite substantial and noticeable in the water

idTips.label: Brown rim
idTips.description: The edge of the bell often shows brown pigmentation, creating a distinct border around the dome

idTips.label: Oral arms
idTips.description: Underneath has a cluster of short, thick arms around the mouth rather than long trailing tentacles

idTips.label: Swimming style
idTips.description: Moves through water with a steady pulsing motion, using its oral arms to help propel itself

habitat: Cannonball jellies are extremely rare visitors to New England waters, typically found much further south along the Atlantic coast and Gulf of Mexico. When they do appear in our region, it's usually in warmer coastal waters during unusual warming events or strong currents that carry them northward from their typical range.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare in New England waters during spring, though any sightings would likely occur as waters begin to warm.
seasonality.summer: Most likely season for rare sightings in southern New England coastal waters during particularly warm years or unusual current patterns.
seasonality.fall: Very unlikely to be present as waters cool, though early fall might offer the last chance for sightings.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters during winter months due to cold temperatures.

funFact: The cannonball jelly's scientific name 'Stomolophus meleagris' literally means 'many mouthed hunter' - and it lives up to this name by having hundreds of tiny mouths scattered across its oral arms rather than just one central mouth like most animals!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, you're more likely to encounter moon jellies, which are much flatter and saucer-shaped rather than dome-like. Moon jellies also have four distinct horseshoe-shaped reproductive organs visible through their bell, while cannonball jellies have a more uniform appearance. Remember: cannonball = round dome, moon jelly = flat saucer.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'cannonball jelly,' this species is actually much more at home in southern waters and represents a true rarity in New England. Most jellyfish identification guides for our region won't even include this species, as it's so far outside its normal range. Any sighting in New England waters would be noteworthy enough to report to local marine biologists.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus found in Atlantic waters, the cannonball jelly is quite distinctive. It differs from other large jellies in our region primarily by its perfect dome shape and short oral arms rather than long tentacles. While other jellies might be large, none have quite the same cannonball-like proportions and compact design.
